settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: Only a 5000ms connect timeout is applied (line 145); this limits connection duration but not target choice.

Exceptions during connect/read are wrapped and surfaced only as an error page (lines 147-156), so direct response-based SSRF introspection may be limited; however connection behavior still leaks reachability.
The parsed content is passed to importProject as a project archive, which may constrain what the attacker can do with the fetched bytes, but does not remove the SSRF nature.
candidates.description: ImportProjectCommand.doPost reads the multipart form field named "url" and passes it to internalImportURL. internalImportURL constructs a java.net.URL directly from the attacker-controlled string and calls url.openConnection().connect() then getInputStream(), with no host/scheme allowlist, no restriction on internal addresses, and no loopback/link-local filtering. Any client able to reach the /command/.../import-project endpoint can make the server issue an outbound request to an arbitrary URL, enabling SSRF (probing internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, internal file/http fetching). The 5000ms connect timeout does not mitigate targeting. This is a candidate; actual exploitability depends on whether the command is exposed without authentication in the deployment (see missing evidence).
missing_evidence: Whether import-project is registered and reachable without authentication: controller.js / module.properties and web.xml (refine.authentication, hf.integration) were not read in this review.
No source line in the inspected set validates or allowlists the URL scheme/host.
Actual server-side network egress policy and available internal metadata endpoints.
preconditions: The deployment exposes the import-project command over HTTP (command registered in a module controller).
The attacker can send a POST with a multipart form field "url" (or the request maps the url parameter).
No upstream network/authorization control blocks access to the command or to internal targets.
candidates.title: Server-side request forgery via import-project URL parameter

counter_evidence: destDir is created by getProjectDir and the code only mkdirs the parent directory if absent (lines 168-172); it does not create the traversal target's parent outside the workspace automatically, so success depends on the target directory already existing.
Behavior depends on whether org.apache.tools.tar.TarInputStream/TarEntry normalizes or rejects '..' names; that library source is not in this repository and was not inspected.
No evidence in the inspected set that gzip/tar contents are validated before extraction.
candidates.description: FileProjectManager.untar iterates tar entries and computes the destination as new File(destDir, tarEntry.getName()) without canonicalizing the result or rejecting names containing ".." or absolute paths. If an entry name escapes the parent directory (e.g. "../../foo"), the resulting File resolves outside destDir and FileOutputStream(destEntry) writes attacker-controlled bytes to that path. The input stream can originate from either the uploaded file (ImportProjectCommand.internalImport, item.openStream()) or the attacker-supplied URL fetch (internalImportURL), so an attacker-controlled archive can drive this path. This is a candidate classic archive extraction traversal.
missing_evidence: The exact version/behavior of the tar library regarding entry-name normalization.
Whether the import-project command is exposed without authentication in this deployment.
Whether any other layer sanitizes tar entry names before reaching untar.
preconditions: The attacker can submit a project archive (upload or via the url field) to the import-project command.
The archive entry name contains traversal sequences or an absolute path that the tar library does not normalize.
The process has filesystem write permission to the resolved target path.
candidates.title: Tar extraction path traversal (Zip-Slip style) during project import

counter_evidence: Only files whose content parses as a JSON object and that end with .json would be returned; non-JSON files would fail parsing.
The module is resolved via servlet.getModule(modname) (line 116), which may return null for unknown names, causing an exception before path use (NPE) rather than successful traversal.
The default module is core and no explicit normalization/sanitization of lang is present in the inspected code.
candidates.description: LoadLanguageCommand.doPost takes the request parameter "module" (defaulting to "core") and the request parameter values "lang", then loadLanguage builds a filesystem path as new File(module.getPath(), "langs" + separator + "translation-" + lang + ".json") using the raw lang string. module.getPath() resolves the module by name via servlet.getModule(modname); lang is not validated against an allowlist of known language codes. A crafted lang value containing path separators or ".." sequences could cause the command to read a file outside the intended langs directory (limited to files that parse as JSON and whose name ends in .json). This is a candidate path-traversal / arbitrary-file-read-read of JSON files.
missing_evidence: Whether servlet.getModule performs any name validation that constrains modname.
Whether the deployment exposes these commands without authentication.
No test or code in the inspected set demonstrates a working traversal payload.
preconditions: The attacker can call the get-languages or load-language command with a controlled "lang" parameter.
A targeted file exists that ends in ".json" and is loadable relative to the constructed path.
The command is reachable without an intervening validation/normalization layer.
candidates.title: Unvalidated module/lang request parameters used to build a language file path
